Title: Vehicle-to-grid power fundamentals: Calculating capacity and net revenue
Abstract: As the light vehicle fleet moves to electric drive (hybrid, battery, and fuel cell vehicles), an opportunity opens for “vehicle-to-grid” (V2G) power. This article defines the three vehicle types that can produce V2G power, and the power markets they can sell into. V2G only makes sense if the vehicle and power market are matched. For example, V2G appears to be unsuitable for baseload power—the constant round-the-clock electricity supply—because baseload power can be provided more cheaply by large generators, as it is today. Rather, V2G's greatest near-term promise is for quick-response, high-value electric services. These quick-response electric services are purchased to balance constant fluctuations in load and to adapt to unexpected equipment failures; they account for 5–10% of electric cost—$ 12 billion per year in the US. This article develops equations to calculate the capacity for grid power from three types of electric drive vehicles. These equations are applied to evaluate revenue and costs for these vehicles to supply electricity to three electric markets (peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation). The results suggest that the engineering rationale and economic motivation for V2G power are compelling. The societal advantages of developing V2G include an additional revenue stream for cleaner vehicles, increased stability and reliability of the electric grid, lower electric system costs, and eventually, inexpensive storage and backup for renewable electricity.

Title: Is awareness of public charging associated with consumer interest in plug-in electric vehicles?
Abstract: Policymakers often seek to increase the visibility of plug-in electric vehicle (PEV) chargers in public locations in effort to build familiarity and interest in PEVs. However, it is not clear if the visibility of public charging stations actually has an impact on PEV demand. The purposes of the present study are to (1) assess the current levels of visibility for public PEV charging infrastructure within Canada and (2) identify whether or not a statistically significant relationship exists between consumer awareness of public charging infrastructure and interest in purchasing a PEV. We use data collected from a sample of 1739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers in 2013. About 18% of Canadian respondents have seen at least one public charger, while the proportion is highest in British Columbia (31%). We find a significant bivariate relationship between public charger awareness and PEV interest. However, when controlling for multiple explanatory variables in regression analyses, the relationship is weak or non-existent. While perceived existence of at least one charger exhibits no significant relationship with PEV interest, perceived existence of multiple chargers can have a weak but significant relationship. Thus, public charger awareness is not a strong predictor of PEV interest; other variables are more important, such as the availability of level 1 (110/120-volt) charging at home.

gold.abstract: This paper investigates the economic impact of vehicle-home-grid integration, by proposing an online energy management algorithm that optimizes energy flows between an electric vehicle (EV), a household, and the electrical grid. The algorithm leverages vehicle-to-home (V2H) for self-consumption and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) for energy trading, adapting to real-time conditions through a hybrid long short-term memory (LSTM) neural network for accurate household load prediction, alongside a comprehensive nonlinear battery degradation model accounting for both cycle and calendar aging. Simulation results reveal significant economic advantages: compared to smart unidirectional charging, the proposed method yields an annual economic benefit of up to EUR 3046.81, despite a modest 1.96% increase in battery degradation. Even under unfavorable market conditions, where V2G energy selling generates no revenue, V2H alone ensures yearly savings of EUR 425.48. A systematic sensitivity analysis investigates how variations in battery capacity, household load, and price ratios affect economic outcomes, confirming the consistent benefits of bidirectional energy exchange. These findings highlight the potential of EVs as active energy nodes, enabling sustainable energy management and cost-effective battery usage in real-world conditions.

These are your colleagues' latest proposals:

--- Researcher B ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b provides engineering-economic equations for vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capacity and net revenue across vehicle types and power markets; it finds V2G economically compelling for peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation, but not baseload.
- Paper-c uses a 2013 survey of 1,739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers; it finds public charger awareness has a significant bivariate link to PEV interest, but the relationship becomes weak or non-existent after controls; perceived multiple chargers is weakly significant, while home level 1 charging is more important.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Paper-c’s weak awareness–interest link may reflect missing economic content: seeing chargers signals infrastructure availability but not private value. Paper-b supplies a monetizable attribute—V2G net revenue—that can be attached to public charging information. Operationally, paper-b’s formulas compute individualized V2G revenue; that revenue signal is added to paper-c’s charger-awareness survey frame to test whether it strengthens PEV interest. Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither paper measures consumer response to V2G revenue or whether public chargers are V2G-capable.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Run a randomized survey experiment with 1,500 new-vehicle buyers, replicating paper-c measures: charger awareness, perceived charger existence, home level 1 availability, and PEV interest. Randomize respondents to control (charger awareness only) or treatment (awareness plus individualized V2G net revenue estimates calculated from paper-b equations for peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation using regional market prices and battery size). Validate revenue estimates against paper-b calculations. Test interaction: V2G revenue treatment × home charging availability. Proposed hypotheses: treatment increases PEV interest more than control; effect is stronger among respondents without home level 1 charging because public V2G opportunity offsets home-charging constraints.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We integrate paper-b’s V2G revenue model with paper-c’s consumer survey design to test whether adding V2G net revenue to public charger awareness increases plug-in electric vehicle interest. A randomized survey among Canadian new-vehicle buyers contrasts charger awareness alone against awareness plus individualized V2G revenue estimates. We hypothesize that revenue information strengthens interest, especially for buyers without home charging, addressing a gap where infrastructure awareness alone is a weak predictor.

FINAL IDEA: Adding V2G net-revenue estimates from vehicle-to-grid modeling to public charger awareness should strengthen plug-in electric vehicle interest beyond charger visibility alone, particularly among buyers without home charging.

--- Researcher C ---
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper-b contributes engineering-economic equations for vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capacity and net revenue across peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation; it shows V2G is economically compelling for quick-response services.  
Paper-c contributes a 2013 survey of 1,739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers showing public charger awareness has weak or non-significant association with PEV interest after controls; home Level 1 charging availability is more important.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Paper-c finds passive public charger visibility does not drive PEV interest. Paper-b supplies a mechanism to make public charging economically meaningful: V2G-enabled public chargers can generate revenue. Instead of awareness as mere visibility, awareness of V2G-capable public charging becomes awareness of a financial benefit, especially for buyers without home charging. Paper-b’s revenue equations estimate per-session V2G earnings that can offset the home-charging deficit identified in paper-c.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Replicate paper-c’s Canadian new-vehicle-buyer sampling and PEV interest measure. Randomized survey with three arms: control (no charger), conventional public charger awareness, and V2G public charger awareness with revenue estimates calculated using paper-b equations for spinning reserves/regulation. Measure PEV interest, home charging availability, charger awareness, and perceived financial benefit. Regression tests interaction: condition × home charging. Hypothesis: V2G charger condition increases PEV interest among respondents lacking home charging; conventional charger replicates weak/no effect. Mediation analysis uses perceived financial benefit. Validate revenue estimates against paper-b cost/revenue parameters.  
Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither paper measures consumer response to receiving V2G revenue estimates; V2G-capable public charger availability and technical constraints are not in source data.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
Paper-c shows public charger awareness alone weakly predicts PEV interest, while paper-b shows V2G revenue is compelling. We propose testing whether awareness of V2G-enabled public charging, using paper-b revenue calculations, strengthens PEV interest among Canadian buyers without home charging. A randomized survey compares conventional and V2G charger conditions, with home charging as moderator and perceived financial benefit as mediator. This links infrastructure awareness to an economic mechanism rather than visibility.

FINAL IDEA: V2G-enabled public charging can convert the weak charger-awareness effect documented for PEV interest into a financial incentive that especially attracts buyers lacking home charging.

Paper B provides engineering-economic equations for V2G capacity and net revenue across peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation, showing economic value only in quick-response markets, not baseload.
Paper C provides survey evidence from 1,739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers that public charger awareness has weak or non-significant association with PEV interest after controls; home Level 1 charging is a stronger predictor.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Adopt Paper C’s finding that home charging availability, not charger visibility, drives PEV interest. Adopt Paper B’s net-revenue equations as a monetizable, market-matched service attribute. Reject the assumption that public chargers are intrinsically V2G-capable; source data do not support this. Qualify colleagues’ framing: V2G revenue can be realized through bidirectional home equipment, so public charging need not be the operative variable. The mechanism is that expected V2G revenue supplies an economic motive that may offset the home-charging constraint identified in Paper C. Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither paper measures consumer response to V2G revenue or availability of bidirectional home charging.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Replicate Paper C survey items: charger awareness, home Level 1 access, covariates, PEV interest. Compute individualized annual V2G net revenue using Paper B equations for spinning reserves and regulation, using battery capacity, daily distance, local capacity and energy prices, and cost assumptions. Randomize into 2x2 factorial: V2G revenue treatment (yes/no) × observed charger awareness (low/high). Outcome: PEV purchase interest. Test treatment × home charging interaction; mediation via perceived financial benefit. Validate by reproducing Paper B capacity/revenue curves for three vehicle types and checking market-type comprehension.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
Paper C shows charger awareness is a weak predictor, while Paper B provides market-matched V2G revenue equations. We test whether personalized V2G net revenue increases PEV interest independently of charger awareness, especially among buyers without home charging. A factorial survey validates revenue calculations against Paper B benchmarks and measures perceived V2G capability, separating economic value from infrastructure visibility.

FINAL IDEA: Personalized V2G net revenue from market-matched grid services should increase PEV interest independently of public charger awareness, especially for buyers lacking home charging, by supplying a monetizable rather than infrastructure-based motive.
transcript.B|1:
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:
- Paper-b provides engineering-economic equations for vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capacity and net revenue across vehicle types and power markets; it finds V2G economically compelling for peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation, but not baseload.
- Paper-c uses a 2013 survey of 1,739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers; it finds public charger awareness has a significant bivariate link to PEV interest, but the relationship becomes weak or non-existent after controls; perceived multiple chargers is weakly significant, while home level 1 charging is more important.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:
Paper-c’s weak awareness–interest link may reflect missing economic content: seeing chargers signals infrastructure availability but not private value. Paper-b supplies a monetizable attribute—V2G net revenue—that can be attached to public charging information. Operationally, paper-b’s formulas compute individualized V2G revenue; that revenue signal is added to paper-c’s charger-awareness survey frame to test whether it strengthens PEV interest. Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither paper measures consumer response to V2G revenue or whether public chargers are V2G-capable.

RESEARCH DESIGN:
Run a randomized survey experiment with 1,500 new-vehicle buyers, replicating paper-c measures: charger awareness, perceived charger existence, home level 1 availability, and PEV interest. Randomize respondents to control (charger awareness only) or treatment (awareness plus individualized V2G net revenue estimates calculated from paper-b equations for peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation using regional market prices and battery size). Validate revenue estimates against paper-b calculations. Test interaction: V2G revenue treatment × home charging availability. Proposed hypotheses: treatment increases PEV interest more than control; effect is stronger among respondents without home level 1 charging because public V2G opportunity offsets home-charging constraints.

WORKING ABSTRACT:
We integrate paper-b’s V2G revenue model with paper-c’s consumer survey design to test whether adding V2G net revenue to public charger awareness increases plug-in electric vehicle interest. A randomized survey among Canadian new-vehicle buyers contrasts charger awareness alone against awareness plus individualized V2G revenue estimates. We hypothesize that revenue information strengthens interest, especially for buyers without home charging, addressing a gap where infrastructure awareness alone is a weak predictor.

FINAL IDEA: Adding V2G net-revenue estimates from vehicle-to-grid modeling to public charger awareness should strengthen plug-in electric vehicle interest beyond charger visibility alone, particularly among buyers without home charging.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:

I reject any assumption that existing public chargers are V2G-capable; neither source supplies this. I qualify financial salience: revenue estimates must include battery degradation and regional capacity prices, not generic savings. Randomized survey of 1,500 new-vehicle buyers using paper-c measures: charger awareness, perceived charger existence, home Level 1 access, PEV interest. Compute individualized annual net revenue from paper-b equations for regulation and spinning reserves using battery size, daily driving, regional prices, and degradation cost. Arms: control (paper-c baseline), charger-awareness only, awareness plus personalized V2G net revenue. Validate by reproducing paper-b revenue/cost sensitivity curves against published parameters. Test treatment × home Level 1 charging interaction; outcome is multi-item PEV purchase interest. Hypothesis: revenue information increases PEV interest primarily among buyers without home charging.

A randomized survey integrates paper-b revenue equations with paper-c consumer measures, expecting strongest effects among buyers without home charging, while validating revenue calculations against paper-b parameters.

transcript.C|1:
SOURCE CONTRIBUTIONS:  
Paper-b contributes engineering-economic equations for vehicle-to-grid (V2G) capacity and net revenue across peak power, spinning reserves, and regulation; it shows V2G is economically compelling for quick-response services.  
Paper-c contributes a 2013 survey of 1,739 Canadian new-vehicle buyers showing public charger awareness has weak or non-significant association with PEV interest after controls; home Level 1 charging availability is more important.

INTEGRATION MECHANISM:  
Paper-c finds passive public charger visibility does not drive PEV interest. Paper-b supplies a mechanism to make public charging economically meaningful: V2G-enabled public chargers can generate revenue. Instead of awareness as mere visibility, awareness of V2G-capable public charging becomes awareness of a financial benefit, especially for buyers without home charging. Paper-b’s revenue equations estimate per-session V2G earnings that can offset the home-charging deficit identified in paper-c.

RESEARCH DESIGN:  
Replicate paper-c’s Canadian new-vehicle-buyer sampling and PEV interest measure. Randomized survey with three arms: control (no charger), conventional public charger awareness, and V2G public charger awareness with revenue estimates calculated using paper-b equations for spinning reserves/regulation. Measure PEV interest, home charging availability, charger awareness, and perceived financial benefit. Regression tests interaction: condition × home charging. Hypothesis: V2G charger condition increases PEV interest among respondents lacking home charging; conventional charger replicates weak/no effect. Mediation analysis uses perceived financial benefit. Validate revenue estimates against paper-b cost/revenue parameters.  
Missing cross-paper knowledge: neither paper measures consumer response to receiving V2G revenue estimates; V2G-capable public charger availability and technical constraints are not in source data.

WORKING ABSTRACT:  
Paper-c shows public charger awareness alone weakly predicts PEV interest, while paper-b shows V2G revenue is compelling. We propose testing whether awareness of V2G-enabled public charging, using paper-b revenue calculations, strengthens PEV interest among Canadian buyers without home charging. A randomized survey compares conventional and V2G charger conditions, with home charging as moderator and perceived financial benefit as mediator. This links infrastructure awareness to an economic mechanism rather than visibility.

FINAL IDEA: V2G-enabled public charging can convert the weak charger-awareness effect documented for PEV interest into a financial incentive that especially attracts buyers lacking home charging.
